newsitem.title: USA: Tax panel plugs draft private activity bond bill.
newsitem.headline: Tax panel plugs draft private activity bond bill.

text.p: An upcoming congressional proposal to give states more flexibility in issuing private activity bonds is getting a plug from a key U.S. House and Senate joint panel, a knowledgeable congressional aide said.

The aide said the Joint Committee on Taxation is telling members of Congress that the draft proposal would cost the U.S. less in the long run than pending bills designed to raise the cap on the amount of private activity bonds that states can issue.
The aide, who asked not to be identified, spoke on a panel at the Association of Local Housing Finance Agencies' spring conference here.

The current cap is $50 per capita or $150 million, whichever is higher, of private-activity bonds annually. Two U.S. House members earlier this month proposed raising the cap to $75 per capita or $250 million.
But the Joint Committee thinks the "revenue loss" for the U.S. from the bill would be "substantial," the congressional aide said.

He said the Joint Committee has concluded that another bill expected to be introduced next week when Congress returns from spring recess is likely to cost the U.S. less and would not create a "new subsidy."
The bill, which is being drafted by Sen. John Breaux, D-La., would relax standards for how states "carry forward" unusued cap allocations at the end of each year.

Currently the Tax Reform Act of 1986 says states can carry forward funds that are unused in a particular year for up to three years. But those states must pinpoint the type of project that the unused dollars will fund in the future.
Breaux' bill would let states fold unused balances into the next year's volume cap.
"The revenue would be less and it's not the creation of a new subsidy -- instead its the enhancement of the current subsidy program," the aide said of the draft bill.

And in a Congress that is sensitive about balancing the U.S. budget, backers of legislation to "simplify or enhance the flexibility" of a program will have a better case that those who want to "enlarge" one, the aide said.
